answer.label: Not Francis of Assisi — an anonymous prayer
answer.sourceLine: Not a documented saying of Francis. This is a line from an English version of the anonymous Peace Prayer, whose French text appeared in La Clochette in December 1912; the translator of this wording is unconfirmed.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Peace Prayer, commonly called the Prayer of Saint Francis
Translator and first publication of this wording unconfirmed

source.excerpt: Lord, make me an instrument of your peace.
trail: Renoux's research ↗ supplies the French text and anonymous publication, not a medieval Francis manuscript.
Wikiquote ↗ places the familiar English prayer under misattributions.
Wintz's Franciscan account ↗ separates the prayer's devotional appeal from Francis's authorship.
source.rightsNote: The exact source or English translator has not been established; no public-domain status is asserted.

externalLinks.label: Renoux: original French and provenance
externalLinks.what: Christian Renoux transcribes the French text, cites La Clochette, December 1912, p. 285, and identifies the original author as unknown.

externalLinks.label: Wikiquote: Francis misattributions
externalLinks.what: The Misattributed section prints the English Peace Prayer, including this line, and explains its twentieth-century origin.

externalLinks.label: Franciscan Media: the Peace Prayer
externalLinks.what: Jack Wintz reports Renoux's anonymous 1912 origin and quotes the familiar English lines.

externalLinks.label: Franciscan Mission Service: the real Francis
externalLinks.what: Franciscan friar George Corrigan explicitly rejects Francis's authorship of the Peace Prayer and dates its publication to 1912.

author.name: Anonymous
author.heading: About Anonymous
author.metaLine: Identity unknown · Author of the French Peace Prayer
author.bio: The French Peace Prayer was published without a signature. Its author remains unidentified; its later association with Francis is not an authorship record.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: The conventional title names Francis, but Renoux ↗ traces the text to an anonymous French publication in 1912.

misattribution.truthLine: Not a documented saying of Francis. This is a line from an English version of the anonymous Peace Prayer, whose French text appeared in La Clochette in December 1912; the translator of this wording is unconfirmed.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: An image can carry an attribution even when no author is named: Renoux describes the prayer being printed on the back of a picture of Francis. His account ↗ distinguishes that visual association from the prayer's anonymous publication and its later explicit credit to the saint.
